output.impression: Tests were administered in English, her dominant language, with norms adjusted for age and education; naming and fluency scores are interpreted with caution in a bilingual speaker. Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile with multi-domain involvement. Verbal memory is impaired: RAVLT delayed recall 5th percentile, immediate recall 15th percentile, and recognition 12th percentile, consistent with an encoding and storage deficit. Visual delayed recall is reduced (Rey Complex Figure delayed recall 8th percentile) with an intact copy. Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 18th percentile) and semantic fluency (Category Fluency Animals, 12th percentile) are impaired, phonemic fluency is low-average. Set-shifting is mildly impaired (Trail Making B, 18th percentile); processing speed is intact (Trail Making A, 42nd percentile). Screening: MoCA 22/30, MMSE 26/30. Geriatric Depression Scale 5/15 (borderline). The profile is consistent with amnestic multi-domain mild cognitive impairment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 26/30 and MoCA 22/30 with impaired delayed recall partly helped by cues, informant-confirmed decline over a year, and preserved instrumental independence (isolated errors compensated by her own checking), staging the syndrome as mild cognitive impairment
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: Bedside testing with cueing and her husband's account of her work, bills and medicines decide whether she has mild cognitive impairment or dementia [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic multi-domain profile: impaired verbal delayed recall and recognition, reduced visual delayed recall, impaired naming and semantic fluency, with mildly impaired set-shifting
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
action_criteria.rationale: A screening score in the normal MMSE range in a woman with a master's degree needs formal testing, interpreted for a bilingual speaker, to define the amnestic profile and a baseline [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TSH, folate, syphilis and HIV serology normal; B12 275 pg/mL low-normal; HbA1c 7.3% above her goal; mild hyponatremia (134 mEq/L)
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid disease, B12 deficiency (eight years of metformin), syphilis and metabolic factors must be excluded or addressed before the decline is attributed to neurodegeneration [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Methylmalonic acid 0.22 umol/L, normal: no functional deficiency
action_criteria.label: Measure methylmalonic acid to resolve the low-normal vitamin B12
action_criteria.rationale: A serum B12 of 275 pg/mL is indeterminate in a woman on long-term metformin with reduced vibration sense at the toes; methylmalonic acid decides whether B12 deficiency contributes [BSH_B12_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild bilateral hippocampal atrophy (MTA 1-2) with subtle temporoparietal volume loss, Fazekas 2 white matter disease and a chronic lacune
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
action_criteria.rationale: MRI shows the medial temporal atrophy that supports a neurodegenerative cause, quantifies the small vessel disease of her diabetes and hypertension, and excludes a post-traumatic lesion, mass or hydrocephalus [NIA_AA_2011] [STRIVE_2013].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio (0.051) with mildly raised p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine as routine treatment for mild cognitive impairment; neither is approved for MCI and the guideline does not support routine use [AAN_dementia_2018].

Do not attribute the decline to obstructive sleep apnea, the remote mild head injury or normal aging alone; the progressive amnestic multi-domain profile with hippocampal atrophy needs follow-up as mild cognitive impairment.
required_recommendations: Disclose amnestic multi-domain mild cognitive impairment with likely Alzheimer disease pathology and a vascular and metabolic contribution to the patient and her husband, explaining that it is not dementia, the risk of progression, and the value of advance planning while she has full capacity [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

Arrange cognitive and functional reassessment in 6 to 12 months and recommend regular exercise (at least twice weekly); explain that no medicine is approved for mild cognitive impairment [AAN_dementia_2018].

Manage the vascular and metabolic contributors to her small vessel disease: glycaemic control (HbA1c 7.3%, above her goal), blood pressure (136/81 mmHg), continued statin therapy, and nightly CPAP use (currently four or five nights a week) [AAN_dementia_2018].

Review safety and work: advise an independent check of the tax returns she prepares for clients or a reduced client load given the recent errors, keep the pill organizer and automatic payments, and review driving at each visit [AAN_dementia_2018].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / vascular contribution to dementia
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 small vessel disease, a chronic lacune, diabetes and hypertension make a vascular contribution likely; the gradual amnestic-predominant course with impaired recognition and hippocampal atrophy, and a decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau when tested, argue against pure vascular cognitive impairment
No visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism, no REM sleep behavior disorder, no cognitive fluctuations described
No early personality change, disinhibition, or executive-predominant profile; memory is the dominant deficit, atypical for bvFTD
GDS 5/15 is borderline and she feels frustrated, but she denies depressed mood, and impaired recall and recognition on formal testing are not typical of depression-related cognitive impairment

differential.diagnosis: Reversible cognitive impairment from thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, or untreated sleep apnea
differential.key_features: TSH 2.8 mIU/L, folate normal, B12 275 pg/mL with normal methylmalonic acid (0.22 umol/L) and homocysteine (11.6 umol/L); partially treated OSA may contribute but does not explain a progressive amnestic multi-domain decline

key_clinical_evidence: MMSE may remain within the 'normal' range in highly educated patients with early AD; MoCA and formal neuropsychological testing are more sensitive at the MCI / mild dementia interface

Mixed vascular and neurodegenerative pathology is common in older adults; small vessel disease does not exclude Alzheimer pathology, and diabetes, hypertension and sleep apnea are modifiable contributors [STRIVE_2013].
A low-normal B12 in a patient on long-term metformin is indeterminate and should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before B12 deficiency is dismissed as a contributor [BSH_B12_2014].

Cholinesterase inhibitors are not approved for mild cognitive impairment and are not recommended routinely at this stage; serial assessment and vascular risk management are the evidence-based steps [AAN_dementia_2018].

key_educational_points: MMSE may underestimate impairment in highly educated individuals; MoCA is more sensitive for detecting early cognitive decline
Vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension) are risk factors for both AD and vascular cognitive impairment, and mixed pathology is common
Amyloid biomarkers (CSF or PET) help when clinical and imaging findings are ambiguous between Alzheimer and vascular causes; one conclusive test is enough
Recognition memory impairment suggests a storage deficit (hippocampal) rather than a retrieval deficit (subcortical/frontal), favoring AD over vascular dementia
Bilingual patients may show asymmetric language decline that should not be mistaken for a focal process
OSA is a modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline and CPAP adherence should be optimized
Vascular and metabolic contributors (HbA1c above goal, small vessel disease, partially treated OSA) are acknowledged and managed alongside suspected Alzheimer pathology

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Dorothy Williams is a 73-year-old right-handed bilingual African American woman who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by her husband, Edwin, for evaluation of memory concerns that have gradually developed over the past twelve to fourteen months. Her husband first noticed the changes when she began misplacing her reading glasses and wallet with increasing frequency, something he initially attributed to stress during tax season. Over the past year, however, he has observed that she occasionally forgets conversations they had the previous day and has twice asked him the same question within a span of thirty minutes, seemingly unaware that she had already asked. She continues to manage the tax preparation work for her remaining clients, but her husband reports that this past season she spent considerably more time than usual on each return and made two errors that she found herself on rechecking, which he says would have been uncharacteristic of her a few years ago; she now checks every return twice before filing. She has also had some difficulty finding words in conversation, pausing mid-sentence to search for a term she clearly knows. Her husband notes this happens more in English than in Spanish, though he is unsure if that is meaningful. About six months ago, she stopped playing golf with her regular group, telling her husband she had simply lost interest, though he suspects she was frustrated by difficulty keeping track of scores. She continues to drive without incident on familiar routes and manages her own medications with a weekly pill organizer that she fills herself, without missed doses. She pays the household bills online, though Edwin recently noticed a utility bill that had been paid twice in the same month; she has set up automatic payments since, and no further errors have occurred. She denies any episodes of confusion, disorientation, or getting lost. There have been no personality changes, hallucinations, or behavioral disturbances. She sleeps reasonably well with her CPAP machine, although her husband admits she only uses it four or five nights a week. She denies depressed mood, though she acknowledges she feels frustrated about the memory lapses. Her appetite is unchanged, and her weight has been stable. She denies headaches, seizures, tremor, falls, or difficulty walking. She was seen by her primary care physician three months ago, who ordered basic labs and an MMSE which scored 27/30 at that time, prompting the referral.
